source_cards.front: Where must you stop at a red light, and how long do you stay stopped?
source_cards.back: At a red light, stop fully at the stop line, or before the intersection or crosswalk where no line exists, and stay stopped while red unless a turn is allowed.

source_cards.front: What must you do before turning right on red?
source_cards.back: A right turn on red needs a full stop first, then a both-ways look with the right-of-way yielded to pedestrians and traffic, watching for motorcycles, bicycles, and mopeds.

source_cards.front: What conditions govern right and left turns on red?
source_cards.back: After a full stop and yielding to pedestrians and other traffic, a right turn on red is permitted unless a No Turn on Red sign or rightward red arrow prohibits it. A left turn on red requires a one-way street leading onto another one-way street, the same stop and yield, and no prohibiting sign or leftward red arrow.

source_cards.front: What must you do at a flashing red light, and what is different at a railroad crossing?
source_cards.back: At a flashing red light, stop fully, yield to oncoming vehicles and pedestrians, and go only when clear; at a railroad crossing, always stop even with no train in sight.

source_cards.front: When may you proceed at steady or flashing red arrows?
source_cards.back: A steady red arrow requires waiting unless a posted sign specifically permits that turn after stopping. A flashing red arrow requires a full stop and yielding to opposing vehicles and pedestrians; proceed in its direction only when clear.

source_cards.front: How do steady and flashing red lights differ?
source_cards.back: At steady red, make a full stop and wait while red continues, except for a permitted turn. At flashing red, stop fully, yield to approaching vehicles and pedestrians, and continue only after the path is clear.

source_cards.front: How do you turn at a flashing yellow arrow?
source_cards.back: At a flashing yellow arrow, turn in the arrow direction when clear, yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians and checking for motorcycles, bicycles, and mopeds.

source_cards.front: What does a green light or arrow allow, and whom must you yield to when turning without a green arrow?
source_cards.back: At a green light or arrow, go only when clear; turning without a green arrow means yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, and letting any pedestrian in the street finish crossing.

source_cards.front: How does turning on a plain green light differ from turning on a green arrow?
source_cards.back: Turning on a plain green light without an arrow means yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, while a green arrow in your direction means going when clear.

source_cards.front: What do you do when traffic signals show no lights at all?
source_cards.back: When signals show no lights at all, stop and cross as at an all-way stop, unless an officer or authorized person directs traffic or portable stop signs are in use.

source_cards.front: What does the eight-sided octagon mean, and who yields on ties at an all-way stop?
source_cards.back: The eight-sided octagon always means stop: halt fully at the sign, line, crosswalk, or curb and wait for a clear way, with every approach stopping at all-way or four-way signs and the left driver yielding on ties.

source_cards.back: Side No-Zones on trucks, buses, and RVs dwarf car blind spots because of wide turns: if you cannot see the driver's face in his mirror, he cannot see you.

source_cards.front: What is the danger of riding in a truck's rear No-Zone?
source_cards.back: Rear No-Zones hide your car from the truck driver and hide ahead traffic from you, leaving no escape at sudden stops; always hold a safe following distance.

source_cards.front: What should you do after passing a truck, and why?
source_cards.back: Front No-Zones punish cutting in too soon or slowing after passing, since trucks need nearly twice car stopping time and room; combinations run up to sixty-five feet and may need over half a mile to pass, so return only with the whole truck front in your mirror and hold speed.

source_cards.front: How do the side, rear and front No-Zones each put you at risk?
source_cards.back: Side zones hide you beside wide-turning trucks, rear zones hide you behind sudden stoppers, and front zones punish early cut-ins.

source_cards.front: How do trucks, buses and RVs turn, and what must you never do?
source_cards.back: Trucks, buses, and RVs swing wide to turn with blind spots up to twenty feet ahead of the cab and about two hundred feet behind; never squeeze between them and the curb or another vehicle.

source_cards.front: How does returning after passing a truck differ from dealing with a turning truck?
source_cards.back: Passing returns need the whole truck front in the mirror at steady speed, while turning trucks forbid squeezing past at all.

source_cards.front: What does towing a light or medium trailer require and change?
source_cards.back: Light and medium trailers ride on safety chains and hitches with large mirrors needed; towing doubles passing, stopping, accelerating, and turning effort, and No-Zones apply.

source_cards.front: How does towing a trailer compare with a truck's stopping demand?
source_cards.back: Trailers double every maneuver's effort, matching trucks' near-double stopping demand.

source_cards.back: Hills with a curb split wheel direction by grade, left up and right down, while hills without a curb always point wheels right.

source_cards.front: Who must wear seat belts in Virginia, and what must a driver do for riders under eighteen?
source_cards.back: Virginia belts every seat: driver plus all front and rear riders must buckle, and whoever drives anyone under eighteen must lock that young rider into a belt, booster, or child seat wherever seated.

source_cards.front: How should a lap and shoulder belt be worn?
source_cards.back: Ride the lap strap low across lap and thighs with the shoulder strap over shoulder and chest, snug, never slung behind the back or beneath the arm; expectant mothers belt lowest on the pelvis.

source_cards.front: Who can waive the seat belt requirement, and what must the waived person carry?
source_cards.back: A licensed physician can waive belting where a physical or medical condition makes it unreasonable; the waived person must pocket the signed statement naming bearer and reason.

source_cards.front: What documentation supports a child-restraint waiver, and what penalties can follow violations?
source_cards.back: A licensed physician may waive child restraints for weight, physical fitness or other medical grounds. The transporter must carry the signed statement identifying the child and the reason. Drivers must secure children properly; a first conviction costs fifty dollars, and a later offense can carry a five-hundred-dollar penalty.

source_cards.front: How must children under eight ride, and when may they ride up front?
source_cards.back: Under-eights ride harnessed in seats or boosters in post-January one, nineteen sixty-eight cars, rear-facing from birth to two years or the maker's bound, forward-facing after, keeping seats or boosters until at least age eight or genuine belt fit, with front seats allowed only minus back seats and minus live passenger bags.

source_cards.front: What must a child show before leaving a booster seat?
source_cards.back: Booster graduation needs all seven: snug lap on upper thighs, snug shoulder on shoulder and chest, tall unsloouched sit, knees bending at the cushion edge, spine flush to the seatback, soles planted, held the whole ride.

source_cards.front: What are the child seat stages from birth to booster graduation?
source_cards.back: Birth to two rides rear-facing to maker bounds, then forward seats and boosters hold until eight or all seven fit tests pass.

source_cards.front: When may a rear-facing seat go in front, and where are younger children safer?
source_cards.back: If there is no back seat, a rear-facing child seat may go in front only when the passenger airbag is absent or disabled. Children twelve and younger are safer restrained in the back seat.
